utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On today, the 14th of March, I wish to bid good afternoon to all those present: The representatives of the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence, some of whom have been here since 8.00 this morning, the two accused, as well as all the staff of this courtroom within or outside it. We need to continue our work today by the testimony of a witness, but before that we need to deal with a question of the admission into evidence of certain documents. So I give the floor to the Defence, who is going to submit their requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to tender the documents shown to the witness according to the list which we produced earlier on be admitted into evidence: Documents under number -- in Chapter 1, "Events"; under number 3, 3rd Corps military police, number 690-2, dated the 24th of January, 1993. There is an English translation for this document, and we should like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit. Also in the same chapter, document under tab 9, 3rd Corps military police, confidential number 09-16, dated the 14th of February, 1993, official record which also has been provided with an English translation, be admitted as a Defence exhibit. Also, the document at tab 11 and the number is 0925, that it be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit. Document number 17, DH1351 ID, for which there is an English translation we should like to tender into evidence. Document at tab 19 that bore the number DH176 ID, should be admitted as an exhibit. Also, a new document at tab 7, 3rd Corps command security sector, number 03/100-112-4 dated the 10th of May, 1993, ERN number 04032452, and it is a daily report for which an English translation has been provided, is being tendered as an exhibit. We should like to tender as an exhibit tab at number 24, also a new document, command of the 3rd Corps, security sector, number 03/100-424-1 dated the 19th of November, 1993, "Information," in view of the fact that there is an English translation. Mr. President, I haven't checked whether some of the documents were signed by the witness. If so, could they be treated as confidential and admitted under seal. But I will check that out. As there aren't so many documents, I'll be able to do that quickly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a document at tab 24, in the second chapter, is the only one signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have checked that that document was indeed signed by the witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you've completed all of your requests. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, please do your duty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The documents will be admitted as Defence exhibits under the following exhibit numbers, and I'll switch to English. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] police, internal number 690-2, dated 24th of January, 1993, is admitted into evidence under the reference DH2076, with an English translation DH2076/E. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, by checking the documents as the registrar was reading the numbers, I have established that the witness also signed document DH2078, so could it be given confidential treatment as well, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, 2078.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document DH2078, dated the 10th of May, 1993, has been admitted confidentially and under seal. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any questions to address, or problems? No problems? Yes, I see someone on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We had a document dated the 22nd of April, 1993, a public announcement by the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and we should like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document is admitted as a Defence exhibit, DK27, with an English version, DK27/E. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can bring in the new witness. How much time does the Defence plan to take with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume an hour and 15 minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Let me check that you are hearing the interpretation of my words in your own language. If that is the case, please tell me so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a Defence witness by General Hadzihasanovic. Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, will you please tell me your name, date, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Semir Saric. I was born on the 6th of December, 1996 [as interpreted] in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us what your current occupation is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a professional soldier currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what rank do you have and your assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My rank is that of captain, and I am a staff officer near Sarajevo, in Butile [phoen] near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what was your position then? And if you were a soldier, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 20th of April, 1992 I joined the TO Staff of Zenica, and until the 2nd of May I was a member of that staff, and then I was mobilised to a military police company of the District Defence Staff of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, have you testified before in an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time for you to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time for me to testify about the events of 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please, captain, read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, before giving the floor to the lawyers, who will start with your examination, I shall give you some information as to the way in which we will proceed. As you know, you're a Defence witness, and for about an hour and a quarter you will be expected to answer questions put to you by the attorneys of General Hadzihasanovic, attorneys that you certainly met before this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Upon the completion of that stage, the Prosecution, seated to your right, will also be asking you questions over a similar period of time, and this is known as the cross-examination. Upon the completion of that stage, the lawyers who questioned you first may have some additional questions for you, which will be linked to the questions put by the Prosecution. The three Judges sitting in front of you may also ask you something at any time; however, the Judges prefer to wait until all the questions have been put to you by the two parties before intervening, because often the questions that they may wish to ask may be put by either party, in which case the Judges will not have any questions for you. But sometimes the Judges need some additional clarification of your answers or they may find that there is a vacuum in something that you have said and then in the interest of justice the Judges may be prompted to ask you to fill in those gaps. You will see that the questions coming from each party may differ. The questions that will be put to you by the Defence need to be neutral, which will require from you quite extensive answers. On the other hand, the questions put to you by the Prosecution may be leading and can be answered with a yes or no. During the period of your testimony, the parties may produce documents and show them to you, and it's quite possible that documents of a military nature, as you were a military man, may be shown to you. The witness will then identify them and comment on those documents. I need also to draw your attention to two important points, the first being common knowledge: Since you have pledged to tell the whole truth, all false testimony is excluded, because, as you know, false testimony is an offence; a second point, which is more technical and rather complicated, is that a witness may refuse to answer the question if he believes that that answer may one day be used against him and incriminate him. In such a very exceptional case, which we have so far never come across, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer. But when he does so, upon the invitation of the Chamber, the Chamber guarantees him immunity from prosecution. As this is a basically oral procedure, as we have absolutely no information about you except a few brief lines of a summary, hence the importance of what you are going to say. As you see a screen in front of you, the words appearing in English will be translations of what is being said in the courtroom, and that will be the record of your testimony. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Should you fail to answer a question -- to understand a question, please ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Sometimes the questions may be very complex and the witness may have difficulty in answering, and the answers are principally intended for the Judges, who have to grasp why it is you have been called and what exactly you have said in answering questions; hence the importance of those answers. Try to be as clear as possible in your answers because, as you know and as I have just said, answers have to be clear to equally clear questions. Should you have any kind of difficulty, please let us know because we are here to assist. I wish to inform you also that every one and a half hours we have technical breaks, which will give you an opportunity to take a rest, because it can be quite tiring to answer questions continuously, but also it will help the technicians to change the tapes, as everything is being recorded. So we will have two breaks in all, of 20 to 25 minutes each, until the end of the day. But according to the schedule, by this evening you should be able to return home. That is all the information that I wish to give you. Without wasting any more time, I shall give the floor to the Defence, who will give you some additional advice and who will begin their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the information provided to you by the President of the Chamber, I would like to give you one more piece of information: The two of us speak the same language, and as soon as you hear my question, you will be in a position to answer immediately; however, both my question and yours also have to be translated so as to enable the Judges and our colleagues in the courtroom to follow what you are saying. That's why I should like to ask you to make a short pause before you start answering my question. Did you ever that?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, what did you do before the war, before the 6th of April, 1992, and where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I was an officer. I worked in Zadar at the Zemunik airport near Zadar, in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you abandoned the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I abandoned the JNA on the 14th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that in 1993 you were a member of the Military Police Company in the District Defence Staff of Zenica. Up to what time did you remain a member of that company and after that did you assume some other duty or did you take a position?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Military Police Company from the 2nd of May, 1992 throughout the existence of that company, which was the 1st December 1992, when the police battalion -- the Military Police Battalion was established, and then I became an inspector in the service of that Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that position, in the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I remained in that position until March or April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you said "the Military Police Battalion," did you imply the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior officer in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: In the Military Police Battalion, my immediate superior officer at first was Mr. Bakir Alispahic and then Mr. Ismet Skopljak and the commander of the Military Police Battalion was Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, what served to regulate the work of the military police in the year 1993, when you were a member of the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The scope of the work of the military police, including the battalion of the military police, were regulated by the -- by the orders for the work of the armed forces, of the work of the security services, the Criminal Code, and the instructions of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber some of the tasks that the military police performed during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The military police had to secure most important facilities within the system of command and control. They had to provide security for military personnel, military documents. They had to regulate traffic. They had to escort convoys of military vehicles. They also had tasks within the crime prevention, such as prevention of different types of crime among the members of military, scouring the ground, protection of communications centres and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that your task was to intercept and prevent certain criminal activities among the members of the BiH army. Tell me, please, whether the military police was also in charge of some other people who were not members of the army, and if that was the case, when was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Are you implying civilians?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the military police did have certain authorities over the civilian personnel but only in case such civilians would perform crimes that fell under the authority of the military courts or when the -- the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina appeared as the aggrieved party of a certain crime committed by civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, could you give us an example of such crimes for which you had certain authority because they fell under the scope of the military district court.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those crimes are regulated by the criminal procedure code that was adopted as the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina and those crimes were crimes against the social order and against armed forces. So when we are talking about the first type of crimes, we are talking about sabotages, serving in the enemy army, and armed rebellion; and the latter crimes, that fall under the category of crimes against the armed forces. They were regulated by the law of the former Yugoslavia, which was adopted as a law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and among them are attack against officers and soldiers of the army. There were some 20 of such crimes which fell under that category of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, when, during what stage of having received information that there might be suspicion of such a crime, at what stage would the military police take charge?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: If we learned that a crime was committed that fell under the authority of the military court, the military police acted immediately, urgently, in keeping with the procedure. However, every such crime of which we learnt and of which we had information, we had to inform the investigative judge of the military court, who would then estimate whether there was any need for him to go to the spot and investigate. If there was no such need, then he would inform the military police. If the judge estimated that the crime was of such nature that it required his presence, in that case the judge would be in charge of the investigation and everything would be done as per his orders, on the spot of the crime, at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you learnt that a crime had been committed, did the military police act independently or did they act in cooperation with other organs?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: If a crime was committed by a member of the army which was prosecuted ex officio, then the military police could act independently, providing they had informed the investigative judge. However, if the civilians were also involved together with the members of the military or if it was only the civilians that committed a crime, then we had to cooperate with members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering my previous question, you said that when the investigative judge or the judge on duty went to the scene, then he was in charge in -- of the investigation and he would issue orders as to what the other participants in the investigations were -- investigation were to do. What would happen if the prosecutor received a report on a crime that was committed? Who was in charge of the pre-criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: According to the law that I've already mentioned, the prosecutor was the one in charge of the pre-criminal procedure, and he could request from the members of the military police to collect the necessary information in keeping with the law so as to enable him to prosecute the perpetrator of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that you worked in one part of the Military Police Battalion. Tell me, what did that part of the battalion specially engage in? That was the service of the military police, as you called it. What did this segment of the battalion do?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the part called the Department for the Services of the Military Police. The military police performs their duties by applying their rules. There are seven parts of the military police, and in this particular part we collected information, we analysed information, and we forwarded that information towards the battalion command and the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to you working in that part of the battalion, could you just briefly tell us how the battalion of the military police was organised in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can comment upon that, the Military Police Battalion had four companies. It had the Department for Services that we have mentioned; and it had the anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please briefly tell us: What was the scope of the work of the companies of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The 1st Company was tasked with performing classical police duties, such as patrols, escorting, the search. The 2nd Company was tasked with providing security. They provided security for command, for institutions, for military documents. And the 3rd Company was to take part in combat activities. And when it didn't participate in combat, it was used for military police work. And then there was the traffic-control company, which was used in traffic, to control traffic, to escort convoys. So its specialty was linked with traffic. The anti-terrorist unit was engaged in controlling military discipline, in scouring the ground, in protecting high military officers who arrived in Zenica. They also provided anti-terrorist protection for various facilities. And there was also the Department for Services. We had the Service for Crime Prevention, where we had inspectors who worked in that service. We also had the escort service, and so on and so forth. We had seven services, and these seven services are how we were organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a member of the service that was in charge of investigation, tell me, please how your service was organised and how many members of staff it had.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I've already said that we had a duty service which consisted of six people and it worked around the clock. We received reports, and we controlled all the other activities. There were between eight and ten crime-prevention inspectors. There were four lawyers, who were in charge of the professional side of the work. They were in charge of filing criminal reports. There were two crime technicians. And I believe that there were six to eight policemen. So all together there were 22 or 23 members of this service. Their numbers varied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you briefly tell us about the chain of command and how it was organised in the military police company of the 3rd Corps. Who were your immediate superiors and who was in charge of the battalion? Who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Ismet Skopljak; the battalion commander was Mujezinovic, and the unit was linked to the corps command through the sector of the security services of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you worked in crime prevention involving members of the army, tell me, please: What authorities did the military police have when it came to the prevention of crime among members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The authorities of the military police were regulated by the rules of work. There were 14 of them. The first one is identification, bringing in, the use of various means, such as means of restriction. And on top of all that is filing criminal reports. Criminal reports were filed to the prosecutor against perpetrators of crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any authority to file criminal reports for other acts committed by members of the army and not only for crimes?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we did not have any other suspicions, you could also file a disciplinary report against an army member who committed a breach of discipline in his place of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, did the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps exist as the only unit of the military police in the entire corps, or were military police units organised elsewhere, in other areas?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion was not the only military police unit in the corps. The brigades also had military police units at their respective levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what was the size of the military police units in the brigades.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I believe that in the brigades that existed in the town of Zenica there were military police units. I know that there were. The mountain brigades had platoons and motorised brigades had military police companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, in the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps, were you superior to the companies and platoons of the military police in the brigades or OGs?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No. It was the officer of that unit who was in command of the military police unit. For example, in the brigades that had their military police units, the commander was the commander of that brigade who was in charge of that unit through his security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any authorities whatsoever over those military police units which did not necessarily have to be the authority of command, of being superior to them?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: We couldn't issue them orders; however, based on our plans and problems of training and education that was drafted by security service Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sector of the 3rd Corps, we participated in the education of the military police units at lower levels and to a certain extent we provided them with the equipment as much as we could, as much as we could spare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, if you learnt that a crime was committed in a certain area, which unit of the military police would be responsible and which one would react and perform their duties in respect of such a crime?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Usually a report about a crime would be received in the duty service of the military police of the 3rd Corps and the Military Police Battalion would inform the investigating judge about this, who would then form a team, as I have already mentioned. So the military police of the 3rd Corps had to carry out on-site investigation, collect traces, secure the site, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Should an event take place in the territory of an operations group or a brigade, who would be responsible for undertaking the steps you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, sometime in June the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group formed its own military police company that was active in the area in order to prevent crime in accordance with the authority of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever an instance that a military police battalion extended aid, direct aid, to platoons or companies in their area if they themselves were unable to carry out their assignment?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was regulated by resubordination of a part of the Military Police Battalion to the military police units of those brigades. I can -- know that I was in the area of responsibility of the 325th Brigade and I was resubordinated to the command of that brigade and asked to assist the military police unit in that area. I was also in the village of Donji Merdani in the area of responsibility of the 333rd Brigade and for a brief period also in Zepce municipality, and I know that my colleagues were also part of military police forces and took part in the protection of certain facilities together with the military police units on whose territories those objects were. Specifically I have in mind the Kraljeva Sutjeska monastery in Kakanj and Guca Gora monastery in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How would you go there? Was this on the basis of a decision within your own competencies, or did you have to receive an order of a superior command?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I think I already said that it was by order that we would be resubordinated to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Saric: In view of the fact that quite a lot of evidence has been produced in this courtroom about, among other things, the existence of the civilian police, tell us what was your relationship with the civilian police. Were you superior to them or subordinated to them? What was the relationship between you?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion was not superior to the civilian police but there was a relationship between us and on two grounds: First, if a civilian commits a crime which is within the terms of a reference of the military court or is a co-perpetrator with a soldier, it was our duty to cooperate directly with members of the Ministry of the Interior; and the second grounds was that members of the MUP, or the Security Services Centre, and the Public Security Station in Zenica, were technically better equipped and better staffed than the Military Police Battalion, so we cooperated on those grounds as well. In carrying out certain activities, we provided technical and professional assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, Mr. Saric: What was the status and resources available to your battalion, in terms of personnel and the ethnic composition of the members of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As far as the personnel is concerned, I can say that there were few among us who had the specialty of military policing, but in addition to our regular assignments, we devoted a lot of attention to training as well. As for equipment, particularly equipment for crime investigation, sometime in June 1993 -- until that period, we only had a single camera. I think it was a Praktika model. And when you asked me about the ethnic composition, I can say that members from the Military Police Battalion came from all three nations living in the area of Zenica, of course in proportion to the population numbers. The largest numbers were Muslims, and Serbs and Croats had equal numbers approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, when carrying out your duties, did you encounter any difficulties? And if so, could you tell us briefly which those difficulties were that you had to deal with, in addition to the fact that you had personnel with insufficient training and lacked the equipment that you needed for your work.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did encounter many problems. First of all, there was a shortage of resources. We also lacked fuel, which we needed to carry out on-site investigations. Another problem was the influx of large numbers of people coming from various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. By way of example, Zenica, which had about 100.000 inhabitants, I think that there were about 50.000 refugees in addition to the population. Among these refugees were men in uniform without insignia and bearing long barrels, and it was very difficult to keep all this under control. Also, members frequently switched from one unit to another, so that in spite of all our efforts, it was difficult to carry out military policing in territory under the control of the HVO. These were just some of the problems that we encountered in carrying out our regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you engaged in the detection of crimes and their perpetrators, tell me, what was the 3rd Corps policies and the policies of its commander with respect to the way in which perpetrators should be prosecuted and law and order respected within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the basis of orders that we received from the battalion command and which came from the corps command, there were strict orders that all perpetrators of criminal offences, regardless of religion or ethnicity or political views, should be treated in an equal manner, and that means lawfully.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me how members of the army were sanctioned, for what kind of acts and what kind of punishment.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Members of the army could be held criminally responsible before the district military court. Disciplinary measures could be taken by the superior command or by the military disciplinary court that was formed at the level of the corps command and in certain specific cases, they could also be held responsible by the misdemeanour courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of all these possibilities for the liability of members of the army and also the problems you encountered in your work, tell me, could you describe this process from the moment you learnt that a crime had been committed to the time when you file a criminal report. Was the procedure identical in all cases, or were situations different?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Of course the situations differed from one case to another. The duty service may receive a report, and the situation is quite clear on the spot. When the perpetrator is caught on site and when the evidence has been preserved, then we can undertake all the other measures, taking the perpetrator into custody, and reporting to the district military prosecutor in this case. However, certain criminal offences were committed by unknown perpetrators. In that case, when the perpetrator was unknown or his identity was unknown, we would secure the traces that we would find on site, collect other information, analyse that information, and then on the basis of analytical assessments regarding the time, the place, the method used, we would make assessments and plans and a certain number of members on the basis of those plans were found, taken into custody, and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, in 1993 did you take part in one such instance of monitoring a certain criminal tendency and finally discovering the perpetrators of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. During 1993, there was -- there were frequent instances of crimes being committed by various members. And I will focus on a case that I was directly involved in, and that is the case of the 3rd Battalion of the 314th Brigade, the so-called Green League. The military security sector of the corps command collected data on the ground and also data we had and those provided by other security organs, especially of the 314th Brigade, and when sufficient information had been collected, sufficient evidence, members of the battalion of the 314th Brigade on the basis of a plan drafted by the corps command, these members were taken into custody, interrogated, handed over to the court with a criminal report and attachments, so all that we had collected over a period of six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the cases when you were able to immediately find the perpetrator and these other cases, when it took you a lot of time to discover the perpetrator, tell me, were you able to discover all the crimes and their perpetrators over that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I think - and this may be my own subjective opinion - that in view of the conditions under which we were working, we had a relatively high percentage of success in detecting perpetrators. But in answer to your question, we did not manage to discover all the perpetrators of criminal offences. And I think that that was not possible anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, I would now like to ask you: In view of the military police work that you described a moment ago and the tasks you had, were you personally ever engaged in certain policework in an area which had previously been the scene of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when this was and could you describe it.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: This was at the end of January 1993 when, with a military police patrol, I was sent to the Lasva village area to take over prisoners of war and to escort them to the KP Dom in Zenica, the prison in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that? Or, rather, could you describe what exactly you did that evening.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was evening. It was dark. It was wintertime. And when we reached the village of Lasva, in front of the school in Lasva we found a large number of civilians and members of the army. And the situation, to say the least, was unpleasant. From the people who were on the spot, we learnt that in combat there had been dead and injured on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With what force did you come to take over those prisoners? And did you transport them from Lasva to the reception centre in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: We reached Lasva in two vehicles, motor vehicles. One was a passenger vehicle; I think it was a Golf A2. And one was a bus -- the other was a bus. The bus had on it 10 to 15 military policemen who had been assigned to this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that the situation was unpleasant. Were you immediately given those prisoners, or did you have to undertake some measures to deal with this rather confusing situation in front of the school where there were both civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: From the crowd, one could hear various cries addressed to us and comments referring to casualties on the army side. So we had to contact with authority, to calm the situation down, and to escort the prisoners to the bus to board them on the bus and to be able to drive them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many prisoners were they, and in what condition were they?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I think there were about 20 prisoners of war, and all of them except one were in good physical condition. They didn't have any visible injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what about this one?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I was told by a military policeman that a prisoner was complaining of pain and having difficulty in walking. I went up to him and saw that he was bent over, that he couldn't walk, and I told the military policeman to escort him to the passenger car, which he did. So I got into that car with him; whereas, the rest of the prisoners boarded the bus and were escorted to the KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you yourself saw him having difficulty walking, did you inquire as to why that was the case? Did you learn why he was in such a state?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did inquire. In the car on the way back from Lasva to Zenica - which took about 15 minutes - I asked him on two occasions what had happened to him. He was not willing to talk. He just told me -- told me that he participated in combat, that he had been injured, but I could not really understand from his answers what had happened to him and I did not really insist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in charge of that particular patrol, can you tell me where you took the prisoners once you took them over.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: We took the prisoners to the KP Dom in Zenica, to the prison there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information before you arrived that there had been dead people on both sides?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No. I learnt about that once I arrived in Lasva. It was then that I learned from the present villagers and soldiers that there had been dead and that the Commander Camdzic and the Commander Rajic were also killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to these prisoners that you took over and transferred to the reception centre for the prisoners of war, did you personally have any other obligations on that evening or on any of the following days?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: On that evening, we did not have any other duties or obligations. On the following day, I learnt from my colleagues who were on duty that the information came from the mortuary of the hospital in Zenica that a few bodies had been taken to them from the theatre of war and that they were there. And we informed of that to the investigative judge of the military district court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally go to the mortuary together with the investigative judge? Do you know who were the judges on duty?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go there personally. As far as I can remember, nobody from the Military Police Battalion went to the mortuary, to the morgue. When I said that we informed the duty judge, I believe that after that the Security Services Centre asked us to help them with the investigation, and I believe that Judge Mirsad Strika established the investigation team, consisting of members of the Security Services Centre and crime technicians of the Security Services Centre of Zenica. So we were not involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, as a member of the military police, or your colleagues receive any orders or tasks in relation to that investigation? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As far as the investigation is concerned, we received a task from our commander to interrogate all of the prisoners about their participation in combat and the way they were captured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to any of them?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were three or four more inspectors who were given the same task. On the following day, I spoke to three prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was it that you carried out your interviews and who were the persons that you personally interviewed, from whom you took statements?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: We performed those interviews in the former JNA centre. This was the place where the Military Police Battalion was billeted at the time. And I spoke to Viktor Rajic, Dragan Rados, and the person whose last name was Kristo, whose first name I can't remember, but I remember him telling me that he worked in the national theatre of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were all of them among those whom you had brought from Lasva to the KP Dom the previous evening?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you conduct your interviews with these persons? Did either you or any of your colleagues use any inhumane gesture, threat, or anything like that during the interviews that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No. To the contrary. The interviews were conducted in a very relaxed atmosphere, I dare say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you interested in the deaths of the persons who got killed on both sides and especially the persons who had been brought to the morgue of the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to what had happened?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: While conducting those interviews with the person that I spoke to, they expressed a certain degree of regret that all this had happened at that moment, they wanted to mitigate their role in the events. They were saying that all this should not have happened, that we had lived in peace until then, and so on and so forth. As for the deaths, none of the persons that I spoke to told me that anybody was killed outside combat. According to the information that I received at that moment, all the persons who were killed in Dusina were killed during combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were three or four inspectors who participated in the interrogation of these persons. Did your colleagues tell you anything about possibly having received different information, different from the information that you received during your interviews?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No. All the information that we received was similar to the information that I received from my interviews. I can illustrate this by giving you an example: Viktor Rajic, with whom I spoke, told me he was the brother of the dead Zvonko Rajic. In addition to him being sad over the -- his brother's death, I asked him how his brother had died. He told me that it was during combat, and that was all. As I have already told you, they expressed regret, and Viktor Rajic asked me at some -- one point whether I could help him and whether I could check whether he would have any problems returning to his workplace in the Zenica ironworks, in view of the fact that he had participated in this particular combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do with the information that you obtained during the interviews with these three people: Rajic, Kristo, and Rados?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I made the official record of these interviews, and I sent that record to the Security Services Centre of the 3rd Corps, and I believe that the information was also sent to the court because an investigating judge was involved in the investigation of that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, did you learn later on how Zvonko Rajic, the brother of Viktor Rajic, had died?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As an ordinary citizen, an ordinary observer, I have learned from the media recently that before this Tribunal Mrs. Rajic, the wife of the late Rajic, has testified and that she has stated that it was Serif Patkovic who had killed her husband. I also learned from the same sources that Serif Patkovic also testified before this Tribunal and that he denied that. Also, somebody called Hakanovic has appeared before the cantonal court in Zenica with regard to the events in Lasva. And as far as I know, from the media again, Mrs. Rajic testified before that court as well, and she stated before that court that her husband had not been killed by Serif Patkovic. So until this day, as a policeman, as an ordinary citizen, I have not been provided with the true information as to what had happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Serif Patkovic? Did you see him on that night when you took over those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I didn't know Serif Patkovic and I didn't see him on that night. Later on I learnt who he was, and I even met him. I know that he was the battalion commander and later on the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to another incident, Mr. Saric. Do you know anything about the kidnapping of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As for the kidnapping of Zivko Totic, like any other member of my service, I received information through the duty service. It was reported to the duty service of the battalion that the escorts of Zivko Totic had been killed and that he himself had been kidnapped. I personally found this information shocking. My colleagues did as well, because we knew these members of the HVO. They were all from Zenica. So we tried to find out who these people were, as ordinary citizens, and we also acted on the report and we informed the investigative judge of the military court, who acted in accordance with his authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did members of the Military Police Battalion or you yourself participate in the investigation or in any activities which might have led to the information as to who had committed this kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, once the duty judge was informed, he set up the investigation team, which consisted of members of the Security Services Centre, and I also believe that members from the HVO police of Vitez and Zenica were there and also the Public Security Station members were there. And on behalf of the Military Police Battalion, my colleagues, Karameli [phoen] and Dragan Rankovic were there, to the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that there was an on-site inspection. First of all, tell me where this happened. In which area of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: This happened on the local road from Zenica to Pobrijezje village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also told us that members of the HVO from the territory that was under the control of the HVO were there. Did you, as a member of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps, have the authority to investigate crimes that were committed in the territory under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No. Once we made an attempt at such an investigation, that was supposed to take place towards the end of December or beginning of January, 1993. I cooperated with members of the Security Services Centre and we were supposed to investigate a murder in Krusctica, which is one part of the Vitez municipality which was under the control of the HVO. We were not able to do that. We were escorted by the HVO police to the place called Vjetrenice, which was under the control of the BH army. From then on, we could not carry out any investigations or any other policing activities in the areas under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the kidnapping of Zivko Totic. Did the military policemen in the battalion receive certain tasks or orders that would lead to the answer to the question as to who committed this crime?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: All the available men in the Military Police Battalion were engaged in the activities geared towards finding Mr. Totic. Some of the members were engaged in escorting joint commissions that were set up in order to inspect the villages around Zenica and the other members were engaged in collecting information on the ground that might have led to the reliable information as to who might have committed this crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that these members of the HVO were your acquaintances or colleagues, because you hailed from the same town. What was the relationship between the members of the Military Police Battalion and members of the HVO and the Croatian citizens of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: We tried to have correct relationships with members of the Zenica HVO, despite certain provocations and humiliations that we experienced at their hands in Travnik and Zenica. We tried to build our relationship as best as we could, and even when conflicts broke out between the HVO and the BiH army, we tried to carry out the disarmament in the most humane way possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain that, Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. A unit of the HVO that existed in Raspotocje, Zenica municipality, and which had been formed a short while before the conflict - I think it was the 1st Manoeuvring Company under the command of an acquaintance of mine and a colleague from work, from Zadar, Juric Jadranko - was stationed there, and I happened to be in the area during those conflicts. I received information that Juric wanted me to surrender to the Military Police Battalion and that he wanted guarantees. In consultation with the corps command, we were able to guarantee the requests Juric made, so he wanted to surrender. He wanted to surrender his weapons and he wanted guarantees for his security and for the civilian population in the area and that the soldiers of the HVO from that battalion should not be taken to the KP Dom in Zenica. In the local community premises, there were representatives of the local community representing both the Bosniaks and the Croats. And I think that on behalf of the Croats a man called Zvonko Akrepovic was present. The weapons were handed over, and all members of that -- of that company were allowed to go home. And the Military Police Battalion during the next 10 days or so secured the area inhabited by Croat civilians, and not a single HVO soldier was taken to the KP Dom. I don't know whether I mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the tasks of the Military Police Battalion with respect to representatives of the International Community and international organisations that were there?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: In view of the blockade of the area, there was increasing demand for food, so the question of hunger became a question of security too, and there were increasing possibilities for a humanitarian organisation which was transporting food to come under attack, so that the food and the goods they were transporting might be looted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any such incident and were you involved in any way -- or rather, the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I personally was not involved in any such incident, but I do know with certainty that at the beginning of September 1993 we received a report that a UNHCR convoy had been blocked in the settlement of Ticici [phoen] on the main road, between Kakanj and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who carried out the blockade?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: A large group of civilians and military men. They blocked the convoy and started taking down bags of flour. When we received that report, a patrol of the Military Police Battalion went there, and upon arrival they met with resistance of those present and there was even a grenade thrown at members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties and did the patrol manage to secure the passage of the UNHCR convoy?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, several people were wounded; some more seriously, some more lightly, members of the Military Police Battalion. And I know that the military policeman Topalovic Dzemal suffered serious bodily injury and he became a 70 per cent invalid. As for the question whether the convoy reached its destination, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to stop there because it's quarter to 4.00. So we'll have the break now, and we'll resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor again to the Defence, but I don't think they have much time left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, before the break you will remember that you explained that your military police patrol was attacked and what the consequences were. My question was whether your battalion's patrol managed nevertheless to escort the convoy and -- to escort the convoy safely to its destination.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you satisfied with the fact that you had escorted the convoy, or did the battalion undertake other measures as well?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: In cooperation with the Public Security Station in Kakanj, or the Security Services Centre in Zenica, worked on the identification of the persons who were involved in the incident, and after operative activities on the ground, the persons who were involved in the incident were identified, taken into custody, processed, and the competent prosecutor's office filed criminal reports against seven persons for various criminal offences they committed: Causing general danger, attacking a military officer while performing his duties, being in possession of explosives and weapons, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Saric, let me go back a moment to some previous questions linked to your duties when interrogating persons captured in Dusina and taken to the KP Dom. Tell me, please: Rados Dragan, was he taken to the KP Dom that same evening by the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that witness Dragan Rados testifying in this court claimed that previously he was somewhere else and that after that he was brought to the KP Dom, what would your response be?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: My response would be that that is not true, because, as I have already said, I interviewed Dragan Rados, among other people, in the place I mentioned, the former JNA club, where the Military Police Battalion was housed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those persons from whom you took statements, where were they taken after that?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: All those persons were taken back to the KP Dom in Zenica again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that during your testimony, Mr. Saric, you mentioned certain locations in Zenica -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Mr. President, I would like to show the witness a map of Zenica, excerpt from set 5, in the scale 1 to 25.000, for the witness to mark the places that he mentioned in his testimony. As I only have one copy, I'd like it to be placed on the ELMO so that we could follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, do you recognise this map? What does it show?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my native town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, will you please take a marker and mark the facilities I will mention and that you spoke about in the course of your testimony, and from that spot will you draw a line and write down what the facility is, and after that I'll ask you to sign the map. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. But where shall I write the name?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where is the 3rd Corps command of which you were the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The command was close to gate number 4 of the Zenica ironworks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you put a number there, an "X" and a number "1".

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And draw a line, and on the white border, write down "3rd Corps command." From "1", draw a line to the frame.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now: The spot where you interrogated these people, the JNA club where the Military Police Battalion was housed at the time or was based at the time.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: It would be roughly here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Put an "X" and a number "2" and a line and write down "The JNA army club."

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now show us the KP Dom, where you took the people from Dusina and where your battalion command was based later on.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please mark Ricica, the locality where the -- no, Raspotocje, where the Military Battalion disarmed this battalion of the 2nd HVO Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is shown on this map, but it is here. This is the beginning of that locality. Raspotocje. But there's more of it off the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now mark where Zivko Totic was kidnapped. You said it was in a street in Pobrijezje.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, here, along this stretch of road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I shall now ask you to mark the position of the district military court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: It is here within this block of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please tell us where the centre of the security services was in Zenica that you said you cooperated with.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: It was somewhere here. The square is called the Bosnia-Herzegovina Square.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you also show us the position of the higher and basic courts -- or rather, prosecutor's offices -- basic and higher prosecutor's offices in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: This is the higher court, and the basic court is very nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And can you also show the position of the music school, please.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The music school -- there's a park here. It was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need a point of clarification. I don't think the witness mentioned the music school at all; although, that was how this set of questions was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. He's drawn it now. I apologise for mentioning the music school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not very serious, because I wanted him to mark it. So it's always useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you now sign the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain, could you on this map point to the hotel where members of international organisations were housed. They must have stayed at a hotel. So could you show us where that hotel was, if you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know. The Internacional Hotel is close to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the witness to date and sign this map with his markings on it, and I should like to tender this document into evidence, and that ends my questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The lawyers for General Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any questions for this witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My name is Matthias Neuner, and I'm appearing here on behalf of the Prosecution, and I will put a couple of questions to you. If you don't understand any of these questions, I'm asking you to tell me that I repeat the question. I'm also prepared to rephrase a question if necessary. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Apart from the 3rd Corps military police, which other MP, military police units were stationed in Zenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I think I said that there were the military police of the 303rd Brigade, of the 314th, and of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You also said that the commanders of this military -- of these brigades of military police would first of all report to the military security staff in their brigades. What I'm asking for is did at some point in the chain of command the brigade's military police also report to the 3rd Corps military police?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I said that the military police within the brigades was under the command of the brigade commander through the military security service. The 3rd Corps military battalion did not have any right to give orders to those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking for orders given downwards. I was more asking for reports going upwards. If military police units of brigades found something out, for example, in relation to the abduction of Zivko Totic, would they convey, would they report that information also to the 3rd Corps military police?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Along the line of reporting, they were obliged to inform the military police of the 3rd Corps. And if we received such information, we would forward it on and act accordingly in line with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In 1993, did you, as a member of the 3rd Corps military police, ever cooperate with the military police of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I personally cannot remember taking part in any action with the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But your colleagues did?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: When you started in the 3rd Corps military police, by mid-January 1993 how many men were there in the 3rd Corps military police?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I believe - and I don't know whether I'm correct or not - that there were between 250 and 300 members at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned there were two chiefs, Mr. Bakir Alispahic and Mr. Ismet Skopljak. Can you just clarify. By January -- or mid-January 1993, who was in charge of the 3rd Corps military police? Mr. Alispahic or Mr. Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me well. I was in the third tier of command. My commander was Zaim Mujezinovic and at one point it was Bakir Alispahic, who was my superior who was in charge of the department. My superior was Bakir Alispahic and his superior was Zaim Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you're referring to "department," you're referring to the Department of Investigations.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Department for Services implies all the services: Patrol, escort, communications, traffic control, security, escort. And I believe that these are the seven services that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Skopljak, can you just clarify. What position did he hold in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: In January 1993, Mr. Skopljak was an inspector in the Department for Services, and then in April or maybe in June he became commander of the Department for Services, replacing Bakir Alispahic in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you yourself served throughout 1993 as an inspector.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Please describe briefly your main tasks.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, my duties as a crime-prevention inspector was when I learned that a crime was committed that was prosecuted ex officio, in cooperation -- firstly, the duty service would inform the duty judge of the district court. And if he wanted us to collect information, we would do that. If the crime was committed by an unknown perpetrator, we collected information and analysed it with a view to detecting the perpetrator. So this would be in a nutshell the duties that I performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Bakir Alispahic was your superior in the first half of 1993. Did he attend interrogations with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he did, whether he was present in the area where we interrogated them. This was a rather large office. He may have been there, but he didn't have to be there. I don't remember whether he was. In any case, we received our orders from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned that sometimes reports would be sent to the battalion command and sometimes directly to the 3rd Corps command. Can you clarify when such reports were sent to the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear the witness saying that he was reporting directly to the command of the 3rd Corps. Maybe my learned friend could explain himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Prosecution, could you please be more precise in putting your question to the witness regarding the reports and where they went. The Defence would like you to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I haven't written down the transcript page. I cannot submit it at this point in time. I think, yeah, I just found it. One second. I cannot submit it at this point in time. I will ask another question, Your Honour. It was on page 15. I cannot give any line. I just wrote this down that on page 15 information was forwarded to the battalion command or to the corps command. I just wanted to clarify this. That -- this was the purpose of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Maybe, witness, you can clarify. Did you never send any reports to the 3rd Corps command, or did this occasionally occur?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No. The department was part of the system of command and control of the police battalion, and all the reports were forwarded via the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic upon receiving a report, to whom would he send his reports? To whom would he forward this information?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: He would forward those reports to the Security Services Centre of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The military security of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And this would be Mr. Ramiz Dugalic? Would he send it to the head of the military security or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Directly to the chief of services.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1993, was the KP Dom also referred to as, and I quote, "collection centre in Zenica"?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The name was not used for the complete KP Dom. There were still parts that were under the jurisdiction of the civilian courts. One part of the KP Dom was rearranged, and it was a reception centre for the reception of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If a document would contain a reference to "collection centre" and not to a "reception centre," to a collection centre in Zenica -- I wasn't on the ground in 1993. To your estimate, to which facility would this document relate to?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I've never heard the term "collection centre" before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned already that prisoners were brought to the KP Dom from Lasva, from the elementary school. Do you remember from which other detention facilities in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility prisoners of war were brought to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the centre for reception of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: The centre was established in June when the first conflicts with the Serbs in Zenica broke out. Then it started functioning. And if there was any need to bring in prisoners of war from wherever, they would be brought to this reception centre. That was a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned in June. Do I take it this was -- you're referring to June 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: No, June 1992, when there were conflicts with the Serbs in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. If I may ask, were prisoners of war from the JNA barracks in Travnik brought to the collection centre? The KP Dom in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were any members from the Zenica -- were any prisoners from the Zenica Music School ever brought to the collection centre, the Zenica KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Again, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So apart from conducting interviews, did you have any contact to prisoners of war at the Zenica KP Dom collection centre?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the prisoners that we had brought from Dusina? Are you referring to these specific prisoners of war? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In general, during your tasks you were engaged in in 1993, did you have any contact with prisoners of war while working in 1993 in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please briefly explain what contact you had.

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: Like in the first case: We took statements that we forwarded to the military district court. We -- we took statements in which we described the participation of these prisoners of war in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you take these statements always in Zenica, or did you occasionally also travel somewhere else to where the prisoners were held in temporary detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: SEMIR SARIC
utterances.text: I took such statements exclusively in the Zenica KP Dom.
